title: Quickstart
text:
The container needs the acquisition geometry, because every reconstruction here is calibrated — the fusion weights are functions of spatial frequency, so the code has to know what a pixel is worth.
import numpy as np
from scatterem import Dataset4dstem

array = np.load("my_4dstem.npy")   # (scan_y, scan_x, det_y, det_x)

dataset = Dataset4dstem.from_array(
    array,
    energy=300e3,                   # accelerating voltage, eV
    semiconvergence_angle=19.7e-3,  # convergence semi-angle, rad
    scan_step=0.25,                 # scan pitch, Angstrom
    device="cuda",
)
scan_step may be a scalar or a (dy, dx) pair. The reciprocal pixel size dk is measured from the bright-field disk rather than taken on faith — see Calibration, which is where most reconstruction problems actually live.

title: Quickstart
text:
Fit the aberrations
The reconstruction needs a decent aberration estimate, and the autofocus finds one by maximising image sharpness. It is a local optimisation, so it needs a starting point:
dataset.meta.aberrations.array[0] = -50.0   # defocus, Angstrom
dataset.determine_aberrations_(correct_order=2)






Give it a defocus



With meta.aberrations all zero the autofocus has nothing to descend from, and it raises rather than silently returning something arbitrary. Any estimate within a factor of two or so of the truth is enough; the sign matters more than the magnitude.
Index 0 is C10, and defocus == -C10.


correct_order=2 fits up to second order (defocus, two-fold astigmatism, coma, three-fold astigmatism). Raise it to reach spherical aberration; the higher orders need more signal to constrain.
The autofocus holds the scan rotation fixed, so meta.rotation must already be right on the way in. If you do not know it, see Calibration.

title: Quickstart
text:
Reconstruct
ptycho     = dataset.direct_ptychography()
dark_field = dataset.tilt_corrected_dark_field()
fused      = dataset.fused_full_field()
Each takes upsample, which defaults to "nyquist" — the factor that brings the output pitch to the resolution the data can actually support, rather than a round number someone picked. Pass a float to override.
All three cache on the dataset, so fused_full_field() reuses the two channel reconstructions if you already ran them with the same parameters.

title: Quickstart
text:
Look at the result
from scatterem.vis.reconstruction_sampling import reconstruction_sampling
from scatterem.vis.visualization import show_2d

fig, ax = show_2d(fused, sampling=reconstruction_sampling(dataset, fused))
fig.savefig("fused.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
Passing the sampling is what makes the scale bar read in Ångström instead of a.u. — and it must be the reconstruction’s sampling, not the dataset’s. The output is upsampled, so dataset.sampling would overstate the bar by the upsample factor: four-fold on the paper’s Fig. 4.

title: Quickstart
text:
Save and reload
dataset.save("carbon.h5")
same = Dataset4dstem.load("carbon.h5", device="cuda")
The file records which fields it contains. If you later add or rename a field on the class, loading an old file fails and names the difference, rather than handing you a half-populated object. See scatterem.io.store.

title: Quickstart
text:
The named datasets
The four specimens from the paper download themselves, verified by md5:
from scatterem import You2026Carbon

dataset = You2026Carbon(root="~/ffstem-data", download=True, device="cuda")
They arrive already calibrated. See Reproduce the paper.

title: Install
text:
pip install git+https://github.com/scatterem/scatterem
Python 3.10 or newer. Ten runtime dependencies, all from PyPI.

title: Install
text:
About the GPU
A CUDA GPU is not optional in practice. The reconstructions are FFT- and kernel-bound, and the NVIDIA Warp kernels that do the direct-ptychography work need one for anything past a small test. Everything runs on CPU, just slowly enough that you would not want to.
If the default torch wheel does not match your driver, install torch first from the index that does, then install this package — pip will leave your existing torch alone:
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
pip install git+https://github.com/scatterem/scatterem
import scatterem initialises Warp, which compiles a few kernels the first time and prints a short banner. That is expected, and it is cached afterwards.






Two side effects on import



import scatterem sets torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("medium") (TF32) and calls warp.init(). Both are inherited from the library the published reconstructions ran under, so results match — but if your own code depends on matmul precision, set it again after importing.

Raising n_batches does not reduce memory

title: Calibration
text: Most reconstruction problems are calibration problems. The fusion weights are functions of spatial frequency, so if the mapping from detector pixels to reciprocal space is wrong, the weights are wrong, and the result is a plausible image that is quietly incorrect. This page is the short list of things to get right.

title: Calibration
text:
The reciprocal pixel size, dk
dk is measured, not assumed. The bright-field disk has a known angular radius — the convergence semi-angle you supplied — so fitting its radius in pixels gives the conversion directly:
\[ dk = \frac{\alpha}{r_{\mathrm{BF}}\,\lambda} \]
with \(r_\mathrm{BF}\) the fitted radius in pixels and \(\lambda\) the relativistic electron wavelength. Dataset4dstem.from_array runs this fit during construction, and the named datasets arrive already calibrated.
The fit sweeps a set of intensity thresholds and takes the median radius, which is what makes it insensitive to where exactly you consider the disk edge to be. It refuses rather than guesses when the pattern has no compact bright region — a fit whose radius exceeds 40% of the detector usually means the input was not an averaged diffraction pattern at all.
dk = dataset.calibrate_reciprocal_from_bright_field()
print(dataset.sampling)   # (dy, dx, dky, dkx)






Counting detectors: pass a hot-pixel threshold



On an event-counting detector a single stuck pixel can dominate the maximum the threshold sweep is relative to, and the fit then locks onto that one pixel. If your detector counts, pass hot_pixel_threshold and check the fitted radius is physically sensible before trusting it.

title: Calibration
text:
The scan rotation
The angle between the scan axes and the detector axes has to be right, and nothing downstream can infer it: the autofocus holds rotation fixed while it fits aberrations. A wrong rotation shows up as a reconstruction that is sharp along one direction and smeared along the other, or as a fused image with directional artefacts that no amount of aberration fitting removes.
If you know it from the microscope, set it:
dataset.meta.rotation = 84.0   # degrees
If you do not, the centre-of-mass field of the bright-field disk determines it: the correct rotation is the one that makes that field a gradient — curl-free — because it is the gradient of the projected potential.

title: Calibration
text:
Detector orientation
Worth checking early, because it is easy to miss and it produces a specific, recognisable failure. If the detector’s axes are flipped relative to the scan, the parallax shifts come out with the wrong handedness, defocus fits toward zero, and the aberration fit reports a suspiciously small C10 regardless of the real defocus. A defocus that will not move off zero is worth suspecting a flip rather than a fitting problem.

title: Calibration
text:
The aberration starting guess
The autofocus is a local optimisation. It needs a starting defocus, and it raises if meta.aberrations is all zero rather than descending from nothing:
dataset.meta.aberrations.array[0] = -50.0   # C10, Angstrom; defocus == -C10
dataset.determine_aberrations_(correct_order=2)
The sign matters more than the magnitude — an estimate within a factor of two is plenty, but the wrong sign can settle into a mirror-image solution with inverted contrast. Through-focus contrast inversion in direct ptychography is physical, not a bug, so a reconstruction that looks inverted may simply be on the other side of focus.

title: Calibration
text:
Scan step and upsampling
scan_step is the pitch of the scan, in Ångström. The reconstruction is upsampled relative to it, by default to the factor that brings the output pitch to what the data can support (upsample="nyquist").
That upsampling is why a scale bar needs the reconstruction’s sampling, not the dataset’s:
from scatterem.vis.reconstruction_sampling import reconstruction_sampling

sampling = reconstruction_sampling(dataset, fused)
Getting this wrong overstates the bar by the upsample factor — four-fold on the paper’s Fig. 4, which is the difference between a correct figure and a wrong one.

title: Calibration
text:
Sanity checks worth running

dk is not the placeholder. If dataset.sampling[2] is exactly 1.0, the bright-field fit fell back and everything downstream is in detector pixels, not inverse Ångström.
The reconstruction is finite. A NaN anywhere usually means a division by a zero SSNR, which in turn means an empty channel.
The bright-field radius is plausible. Print it. A radius near the detector half-width, or a couple of pixels, both mean the fit found the wrong thing.
Both channels look sensible on their own before you read the fused result. Fusion cannot rescue a channel that failed; it will just weight it down and leave a band with nothing in it.

title: scatterem
text:
A 4D-STEM dataset holds more information than any single reconstruction recovers. Direct ptychography reads the phase gradient encoded in the bright-field disk and recovers low and mid spatial frequencies with high efficiency, but its transfer falls away past the disk. Tilt-corrected dark field reads the parallax shift of scattering outside the disk and recovers high frequencies, but carries almost nothing at low ones. Neither channel spans the band on its own, and used alone each leaves a gap where the other is strong.
Fused full-field STEM combines them as an SSNR-weighted Wiener fusion, so each spatial frequency is taken from whichever channel measures it better. The result is one image with no missing band.
Run it now on a free GPU: the notebook installs the package, fetches one dataset from Zenodo and reconstructs it, with nothing to set up locally.
That is the whole pipeline. Each channel is also available on its own — dataset.direct_ptychography() and dataset.tilt_corrected_dark_field() — and all three share one calibration, so they land on the same grid.

title: scatterem
text:
Scope
This repository is the FF-STEM pipeline: direct ptychography, tilt-corrected dark field, their fusion, and the calibration and I/O they need. The wider scatterem codebase covers iterative ptychography, tomography and multislice simulation; those parts accompany their own publications and are released with them.

direct_ptychography(dataset: scatterem.utils.data.datasets.Dataset4dstem | scatterem.utils.data.datasets.DatasetVirtualBrightField4dstem, upsample: Union[float, str] = 'nyquist', bright_field_mask_threshold: float = 0.5, verbosity: int = 0, n_batches: int = 25, return_snr: bool = False, phase_sign: Literal['preserve', 'positive', 'negative'] = 'positive', ssnr_method: str = 'analytical', **kwargs) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor | None]
Performs a joint ptychography reconstruction and aberration determination. Args: dataset: Dataset4dstem or DatasetVirtualBrightField4dstem object containing the diffraction pattern. upsample: Upsampling factor for the diffraction pattern. bright_field_mask_threshold: Threshold for the bright field. verbosity: Verbosity level. n_batches: Number of batches for the vBF. return_snr: Whether to compute the ptychography SSNR (method selected by ssnr_method). phase_sign: Resolve the global phase sign ambiguity. “positive” flips negative-skew phase images so atom columns are positive, “negative” enforces the opposite sign, and “preserve” leaves the raw direct-ptycho sign unchanged. ssnr_method: How to compute the SSNR when return_snr is True. “analytical” (default) uses the phase-contrast-transfer-function noise model (CTF-aware: ptycho SSNR -> 0 at low q, no DC/low-q transfer); “empirical” reconstructs a checkerboard BF half-split and forms the raw half-difference power ratio (data-driven, better at high dose).
Returns: torch.Tensor: The reconstructed phase image (Imaginary part). torch.Tensor | None: The SNR of the reconstructed phase image if return_snr is True, otherwise None.
Raises: ValueError: If the dataset is not a valid Dataset4dstem object. ValueError: If the upsample is invalid.


tilt_corrected_dark_field
tilt_corrected_dark_field(dataset: scatterem.utils.data.datasets.Dataset4dstem, n_dark_field_segments: int = 32, verbosity: int = 0, bright_field_mask_threshold: float = 0.3, upsample: Union[float, str] = 'nyquist', return_snr: bool = False, snr_blur_sigma: float = 0.0, shift_method: str = 'drizzle', drizzle_pixfrac: float = 1.0, drizzle_kde_sigma: float = 0.0) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor | None]
Tilt-corrected dark-field reconstruction.
shift_method selects how each azimuthal dark-field segment is sub-pixel shifted (by its parallax shift) and accumulated onto the up-sampled grid:

"drizzle" (default) — area-overlap drizzle (box splat + hit-map normalization). Non-negative and ringing-free, which is the physically correct behaviour for counting data: at low dose the segment images are single electron counts and Fourier shifting turns each into a sinc with ~20% negative side-lobes. drizzle_pixfrac sets the drop size (fraction of an input pixel; 1.0 fills the grid from one frame) and drizzle_kde_sigma optionally Nadaraya-Watson-smooths sparse holes.
"fourier" — Fourier zero-pad upsample + phase-ramp shift. Marginally sharper on dense, well-sampled (high-dose) data, but rings on sparse data.

You2026Gd2O3

Aberrations
scatterem.utils.aberration_basis

cartesian_chi
cartesian_chi(qy: 'Tensor', qx: 'Tensor', wavelength: 'float', coefficients: 'Sequence[float] | Tensor') -> 'Tensor'
Evaluate the aberration phase chi in radians.
Args: qy: reciprocal-space y coordinates, in inverse Angstrom. qx: reciprocal-space x coordinates, same shape as qy. wavelength: electron wavelength in Angstrom (see :func:scatterem.utils.physics.electron_wavelength). coefficients: the 12 cartesian coefficients in :data:COEFFICIENT_NAMES order, in Angstrom.
Returns: chi with the broadcast shape of qy and qx.


cartesian_to_polar
cartesian_to_polar(cartesian: 'Dict[str, float]') -> 'Dict[str, float]'
Convert cartesian aberration pairs to magnitude and angle.
The magnitude is non-negative and the angle is the one that satisfies C * cos(m * (phi - phi_m)) == Ca * cos(m*phi) + Cb * sin(m*phi), so the returned pair describes the same wavefront as its input. Missing entries are taken as zero.
The angle is only determined modulo 2*pi/m – an m-fold term is physically unchanged by such a rotation – and is returned in the branch atan2 gives, i.e. within +-pi/m.


polar_to_cartesian
polar_to_cartesian(polar: 'Dict[str, float]') -> 'Dict[str, float]'
Convert magnitude/angle aberrations to the cartesian pairs.
Missing entries are taken as zero, so a caller may pass only the coefficients it cares about.

Calibration helpers
scatterem.utils.data.disk_fit

fit_bright_field_disk
fit_bright_field_disk(dp, *, threshold_range: 'Tuple[float, float]' = (0.25, 0.75), n_thresholds: 'int' = 100, max_radius_fraction: 'float' = 0.4, min_contrast: 'float' = 3.0) -> 'Tuple[float, NDArray]'
Radius and centre of the central bright-field disk, in pixels.
Args: dp: 2D averaged diffraction pattern (torch tensor or numpy array). threshold_range: low and high sweep limits as fractions of the spike-free maximum. Keep it symmetric about 0.5 – that symmetry is what makes the median unbiased. Widen it for a very soft edge. n_thresholds: number of thresholds in the sweep. max_radius_fraction: reject a fit whose radius exceeds this fraction of the smaller detector dimension. Guards against “fitting” a pattern that has no compact disk, where the sweep returns a radius of order the detector itself. min_contrast: reject a fit whose median intensity inside the disk is not at least this many times the median outside it.
Returns: (radius, centre) with radius in pixels as a float and centre as a 2-element numpy array ordered [y, x].
Raises: ValueError: if dp is not 2D, or if the pattern contains no identifiable bright-field disk.

title: API reference
text:
Physics
scatterem.utils.physics

electron_wavelength
electron_wavelength(accelerating_voltage: 'float') -> 'float'
Return the relativistic electron wavelength in Angstrom.
An electron accelerated through V volts gains kinetic energy eV. Its momentum follows from the relativistic energy-momentum relation, and the de Broglie relation turns that into a wavelength::
lambda = h / sqrt(2 m0 e V (1 + e V / (2 m0 c^2)))
The bracketed factor is the relativistic correction; it is negligible below a few hundred volts and reaches ~1.2 at 200 kV, where ignoring it would overstate the wavelength by roughly 10%.
Args: accelerating_voltage: the accelerating voltage in volts (e.g. 200e3 for a 200 kV microscope). Must be positive.
Returns: The wavelength in Angstrom.
Raises: ValueError: if accelerating_voltage is not positive.

title: API reference
text:
Grids
scatterem.utils.grids

fft_frequencies_2d
fft_frequencies_2d(shape: 'Sequence[int]', sampling: 'Sequence[float]' = (1.0, 1.0), half_pixel_shift: 'bool' = False, device: 'str | torch.device' = 'cpu', dtype: 'torch.dtype | None' = None) -> 'Tensor'
Stacked (qy, qx) FFT frequencies for a 2D grid.
Args: shape: grid dimensions (ny, nx). sampling: real-space pixel size (dy, dx); frequencies come out in the reciprocal of whatever unit this is given in. half_pixel_shift: offset both axes by half a frequency bin. Use for quantities defined on pixel centres rather than pixel edges. device: device for the returned tensor. dtype: floating dtype for the returned tensor; torch’s default if omitted.
Returns: A tensor of shape (2, ny, nx) whose first slice is qy and second is qx, matching torch.fft axis order.


radial_average
radial_average(image, sampling: 'Sequence[float]')
Radial average of a corner-origin 2D array, over FFT frequency bins.
Replaces utils/utils.radial_average2, which is a py4DSTEM (GPL-3.0) derivative. Written here from the definition instead.
Each pixel contributes to the two bins its |q| falls between, in proportion to how close it lies to each — a linear (area-weighted) partition rather than nearest-bin assignment, which is what keeps a radial profile from developing sawtooth ripple at small radii where few pixels land per bin. The two contributions are accumulated in one pass by concatenating them, so the normalising count and the weighted sum each need a single bincount.
Args: image: 2D array with the zero frequency at [0, 0], as torch.fft produces. numpy array or torch tensor. sampling: real-space pixel size (dy, dx); the returned frequencies are in the reciprocal of that unit.
Returns: (q_bins, profile), truncated to the largest frequency represented on both axes so the tail is not built from corner pixels alone.
One deliberate difference from the replaced function: it truncated at the x axis maximum only, so with anisotropic sampling it returned bins past the shorter axis’ Nyquist, where a “ring” is really a pair of corner wedges. This truncates at the smaller of the two. On a square grid with equal sampling — every case the published figures use — the two agree to machine precision (measured max abs difference 2e-15, same bin count); with anisotropic sampling this returns a shorter profile, which matters to a caller slicing the result by index.

Colour an image, using phase as hue when it is given.

lightness is fixed so the bar reads as hue alone. The default sits near the middle of the range where the sRGB gamut is widest, so the wheel keeps its chroma all the way round instead of desaturating at some hues.


tile_to_rgba
tile_to_rgba(rows, *, norm=None, cmap: 'str' = 'gray', chroma: 'float' = 0.13) -> 'NDArray'
Composite a grid of same-shaped images into one RGBA mosaic.
Replaces list_of_arrays_to_rgba. Each entry is coloured independently and the results are tiled, so a bright panel cannot darken its neighbours – the alternative, one normalisation across the whole grid, makes every panel but the brightest unreadable.
Args: rows: sequence of rows, each a sequence of same-shaped 2D arrays. norm: callable mapping amplitude to [0, 1], applied to each panel. If omitted, each panel is scaled by its own finite min and max.

    requires ``[0, 1]`` and *clips*, so handing it raw data silently

chroma: Oklab chroma for the phase hue of complex panels.

Sampling describing one pixel of a reconstructed image.
The scan covered scan_px * scan_step of specimen; the reconstruction represents that same extent with image_px pixels, so::
pixel_size = scan_step * scan_px / image_px
which needs no knowledge of the upsample factor that was requested – it reads the factor off the result. That matters because upsample="nyquist" picks the factor from the data, so the caller may not know what it was.

Carbon is the one to run first: smallest download, about a second of reconstruction, and it exercises the whole pipeline.






Fitting a smaller GPU



Fig4_diffraction.py takes scan_edge_crop, which trims the scan and so shrinks the output. The paper uses 128 (256² scan → 1024² output, 17.6 GiB); 192 gives 128² → 512² at 4.4 GiB, which is what the Colab notebook runs; 224 gives 64² → 256² at 2.5 GiB.
Reducing the scan is the lever that works. Raising n_batches increases peak memory — measured 17.6, 21.0 and 24.5 GiB for 15, 60 and 150 batches, with bit-identical output.

title: Reproduce the paper
text:
What each script does
The same five steps, with per-specimen parameters:

Construct the named dataset, which downloads, verifies, and calibrates dk from the bright-field disk.
Set the scan rotation, and a starting defocus for the autofocus.
determine_aberrations_ — fit aberrations by sharpness, rotation held fixed.
Reconstruct all three channels.
Save each with a physical scale bar.

Reading one script is enough to see how to apply the pipeline to your own data; Quickstart is the same thing without the paper’s parameters.

title: Reproduce the paper
text:
Verifying your run
Each script prints a summary line and asserts the things that quietly go wrong:
[Fig2-carbon] OK: dp(96, 96) tcdf(96, 96) fff(96, 96) dk=0.042126 finite=True
dk must not be 1.0 — that is the uncalibrated placeholder, and it means the bright-field fit fell back. finite=True means no NaNs, which otherwise indicate a channel that produced nothing and a division by a zero SSNR.

title: Reproduce the paper
text:
Comparison plots
Where a reference is available — a simulated potential for carbon, a phantom for Co₃O₄ — the scripts also emit a side-by-side comparison. Those references are not in the Zenodo record, so the scripts skip that step and say so rather than failing:
[Fig2-carbon] reference carbon72_potential.npy not found; skipping comparison plot.

title: Reproduce the paper
section: Numerical differences from the published figures
text:
Numerical differences from the published figures
Two are worth knowing about.
The bright-field disk fit is an independent implementation, and end to end through the crop-and-refit it lands within 0.152% of the original dk. That shifts the reciprocal scale by well under the uncertainty on the convergence angle itself, but it is not bit-identical.
Scale-bar lengths are chosen on a 1-2-5 ladder, so a bar may be a different round number than in the paper — 10 Å where the paper shows 5 Å on the same field, for instance. The bar is correct; only which round number it picks differs.

title: The method
text:
A converged probe illuminates a specimen and a pixelated detector records the full diffraction pattern at every scan position. What reaches the detector splits naturally in two, and the split is where the method starts.
Inside the bright-field disk, the transmitted beam interferes with itself. Weak-phase scattering shifts the intensity distribution across the disk in proportion to the local phase gradient, which is what single-side-band ptychography reads. That works beautifully at low and mid spatial frequencies — each frequency is measured by a pair of overlapping beams, and the overlap is large — but the overlap shrinks as the spatial frequency approaches twice the convergence angle, and past it there is none. Transfer falls to zero.
Outside the disk, scattering is incoherent to good approximation, and a dark-field detector segment sees an image that shifts with defocus and with the segment’s angle — a parallax. Correcting those shifts and summing recovers high spatial frequencies well. But a dark-field segment carries almost no low-frequency information: at low frequency the parallax shift is small and the signal is dominated by thickness and composition rather than phase.
So each channel is strong exactly where the other is weak. Neither spans the band.

title: The method
text:
A converged probe illuminates a specimen and a pixelated detector records the full diffraction pattern at every scan position. What reaches the detector splits naturally in two, and the split is where the method starts.
Inside the bright-field disk, the transmitted beam interferes with itself. Weak-phase scattering shifts the intensity distribution across the disk in proportion to the local phase gradient, which is what single-side-band ptychography reads. That works beautifully at low and mid spatial frequencies — each frequency is measured by a pair of overlapping beams, and the overlap is large — but the overlap shrinks as the spatial frequency approaches twice the convergence angle, and past it there is none. Transfer falls to zero.
Outside the disk, scattering is incoherent to good approximation, and a dark-field detector segment sees an image that shifts with defocus and with the segment’s angle — a parallax. Correcting those shifts and summing recovers high spatial frequencies well. But a dark-field segment carries almost no low-frequency information: at low frequency the parallax shift is small and the signal is dominated by thickness and composition rather than phase.
So each channel is strong exactly where the other is weak. Neither spans the band.

title: The method
The method
text:
Sub-pixel accumulation
Tilt-corrected dark field shifts each azimuthal segment by its parallax shift and accumulates. How that shift is applied matters at low dose, and there are two options.
shift_method="fourier" zero-pads and applies a phase ramp. It is exact for dense, band-limited signals.
shift_method="drizzle" (the default) treats each input pixel as a small square drop, places it at the shifted position, and distributes its flux to the output pixels it overlaps by area — the drizzle of Fruchter & Hook (2002), specialised to pure translations on a regular grid. Because every weight is non-negative, the result is non-negative for non-negative input, and flux is conserved exactly.
The difference shows up when the frames are sparse. At very low dose a segment image is a handful of single electron counts, and Fourier shifting turns each isolated count into a sinc: roughly 20% negative side-lobes, with energy spread across the whole frame. Drizzle has no ringing to spread.






Note



The paper’s figures were produced with the Fourier path; drizzle came afterwards. Both are available, and on dense high-dose data they agree closely — on amorphous carbon the fused images correlate to 0.9992.

title: The method
text:
What this is not
The direct ptychography here is non-iterative. It is a single linear inversion of the bright-field intensity, not a phase-retrieval loop, so it has no convergence behaviour, no step size and no initialisation beyond the aberration estimate. That is why it runs in under a second on a 96² scan. It also means it inherits the weak- phase approximation: strong scatterers and thick specimens depart from it, and an iterative multislice reconstruction will do better there.

text:

Single-side-band ptychography: Rodenburg & Bates (1992); Pennycook et al. (2015)
Tilt-corrected bright/dark field and parallax: Ophus et al. (2016)
Drizzle: Fruchter & Hook, PASP 114, 144 (2002)
Sub-pixel registration: Guizar-Sicairos, Thurman & Fienup, Opt. Lett. 33, 156 (2008)
